title: Ask Devin · Trace code before making a change
summary: Find the file that makes a decision. Follow its caller before you plan an edit.

intro.what: Ask reads an index, a map of the files in a project. You can ask how two files fit together without starting a cloud coding machine.
intro.features: Ask for a file link beside each claim. In Plan mode, ask which files a change would touch and which test would prove it.
intro.exchange: Trace a mail report from a row count to the rule that skips empty rows.
intro.m365: Find the file that picks the columns in a team roster.
intro.developer: Follow a game button from the click to the score rule.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: Ask for a file link beside each claim. In Plan mode, ask which files a change would touch and which test would prove it.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: Choose Ask and select an indexed practice project. A repository, or repo, is a project stored with its change history.
Ask “Which file decides the score? Link to the rule and to one place that calls it.”
Open both links. Read the named rule and check that the other file really calls it. Stay in Ask while you plan.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: An answer in Ask does not edit a file or run the test for you. Start an Agent session when you want the plan carried out.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-ask.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: An old index can describe an earlier rule. Check the branch and the lines in the link before you rely on the answer.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: Read Ask Devin for planning and handoff. Read Index a Repository if the project is missing.

title: Agent Sessions · Make a change and test it
summary: Give a cloud session one small job and a test you can check yourself.

intro.what: An agent is a helper that can act. A cloud session gives it a separate computer to read files, edit code and run tests.
intro.features: Devin can show its work and open a pull request, or PR. A PR is a proposed change that someone can inspect before it joins the main code.
intro.exchange: Test a report with a pretend mailbox that has no owner.
intro.m365: Fix a label in a sample meeting list and check the page.
intro.developer: Change one game rule on a branch and play a round.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: Devin can show its work and open a pull request, or PR. A PR is a proposed change that someone can inspect before it joins the main code.
A branch lets you try a change on a separate line of work. You can test there before anyone merges the change into the shared copy.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: Start a new session in Agent mode. Pick a practice repo where you can propose changes.
Ask Devin to add a label to a test page, run its check and open a draft PR. A draft tells teammates the change is still being checked.
Open the changed file and the test output. Compare both with the job you gave it.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: A passing test only covers the case it tried. The agent cannot open a PR if its Git access is read-only.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-agent.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: A session message saying “done” is easy to skim. Check the actual branch, test result and PR before accepting the change.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: Use Your First Session to pick Agent mode. The GitHub integration guide explains which repos the agent can use.

title: DeepWiki · Follow a diagram back to its source
summary: Start with a map of a project, then open the file that proves one arrow.

intro.what: DeepWiki turns indexed project files into a wiki, a set of linked pages about the code.
intro.features: Its pages can include a diagram, a short explanation and links to source files. A link lets you compare the map with what the code says.
intro.exchange: Look up the part of a mail report that makes the final table.
intro.m365: Trace how a sample form sends a response to a list.
intro.developer: Find the file that loads questions for a quiz.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: Its pages can include a diagram, a short explanation and links to source files. A link lets you compare the map with what the code says.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: Open DeepWiki for an indexed practice repo. Pick a page about a feature you know.
Find one arrow or sentence about two parts of the app. Follow its source link and look for the call in the file.
If an arrow has no link, follow the page’s source links. Ask Devin to find the exact call if you still need it.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: A diagram can explain the intended path. It cannot show that a particular job ran or that a test passed yesterday.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-deepwiki.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: Read the linked revision. A good map from last week can still show an old name after someone moves a file.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: Read DeepWiki for diagrams and citations. Read Index a Repository to see how a repo becomes available for the wiki.

title: Devin Review · Check a finding on a pull request
summary: Test a review comment against the changed lines before you act on it.

intro.what: Review reads a diff, the lines a PR adds or removes. It groups changes and points out possible bugs.
intro.features: Ask for a one-time review or set up automatic reviews. Each finding points to code you can inspect.
intro.exchange: Try the empty-row case when a mailbox export rule changes.
intro.m365: Check whether a changed list filter still includes a blank owner.
intro.developer: Play a tie round after a score rule changes.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: Ask for a one-time review or set up automatic reviews. Each finding points to code you can inspect.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: Open a practice PR in a connected repo. Post /devin review as a new PR comment.
Open the review and find the line linked to a finding. Write down the input that would make it fail.
Run that input on the proposed change. If there is no finding, still try the boundary case yourself.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: A finding can be mistaken. An empty list of findings cannot prove the change is bug-free.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-review.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: Check the commit the review examined. If new changes arrived, request a review of the latest commit before closing a finding.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: The Review guide covers findings and repeat reviews. The GitHub integration guide explains comments that request changes.

title: Skills · Save a recipe that Devin can repeat
summary: Give a repeated task a name. Try the same recipe on two small samples.

intro.what: A skill is a file of instructions for one job. It can tell Devin which facts to read and what the result should look like.
intro.features: Keep a repo skill at .agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. Use @skills:<name> in a cloud prompt to call it by name. Older guides call these recipes Playbooks.
intro.exchange: Give a weekly mail count the same headings each time.
intro.m365: Turn meeting notes into a list of decisions and owners.
intro.developer: Test the reset button after every change to a game.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: Keep a repo skill at .agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. Use @skills:<name> in a cloud prompt to call it by name. Older guides call these recipes Playbooks.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: In a practice repo, create .agents/skills/count-ready/SKILL.md. Copy the starter file into it and commit it. The header names the skill. The last line gives it a rule.
Once the skill is available, send “@skills:count-ready Labels: ready, waiting, ready.”
Check for a count of two. Change one label and call the same skill again.
sections.practiceCode:
---
name: count-ready
description: Count rows marked ready.
---
Read the labels in the request. Count only rows marked ready. Give the count and their names.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: A saved recipe cannot supply missing input or grant access to a file the session cannot read.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-skills.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: Use the exact skill name when testing. A result that looks right once does not prove the session used the saved rule.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: The Skills guide gives the file layout and call syntax. Creating Playbooks explains the older form you may still see.

title: Blueprints & Snapshots · Start with the tools ready
summary: Build the workbench once and check what the next session finds on it.

intro.what: A blueprint lists what to install. A build follows the list and saves a snapshot, a ready-to-start copy of the work machine.
intro.features: The snapshot can hold the runtime that runs the code and the packages the project needs. Each new session gets a fresh copy.
intro.exchange: Prepare the tools that read a made-up mail report.
intro.m365: Put the library for a sample roster export in the saved setup.
intro.developer: Start a new game project with its test runner ready.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: The snapshot can hold the runtime that runs the code and the packages the project needs. Each new session gets a fresh copy.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: Open Settings, then Environment for a practice repo. Read the blueprint and find the command that installs the test tool.
After an approved practice build shows Success in Snapshots, start a new session and ask for the tool’s version.
Run a small project test. A printed version checks the install. A passing test checks that the project can use it.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: Installing a tool inside one running session does not add it to the saved snapshot. Change the blueprint and build it again.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-blueprints.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: Check which snapshot is active before comparing two sessions. An older session may still be using the previous setup.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: Read Environment Blueprints for build steps. Environment Setup explains where to check repository access and active setup.

unverified: A fixed startup time for every session.

title: Devin CLI · Hand a local task to the cloud
summary: Start a check at your keyboard and find the same task on the cloud machine.

intro.what: The Devin CLI runs in a terminal, a window where you type commands. Start it in the folder that holds your code.
intro.features: The /handoff command sends the current branch, conversation and pending code changes to a cloud session. You can follow the job after you close the laptop.
intro.exchange: Hand off a slow test of a fake mailbox export.
intro.m365: Run a sample list check locally before handing over its longer test.
intro.developer: Try a small score change locally and have the cloud run the game tests.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: The /handoff command sends the current branch, conversation and pending code changes to a cloud session. You can follow the job after you close the laptop.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: Open a terminal in a connected practice repo. Start the installed CLI with devin and ask it to identify the current branch.
Check the changed files for anything you do not want to send. At the Devin prompt enter /handoff followed by one small test request.
Open the cloud session it creates. Check the branch and the test result.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: A handoff starts a fresh cloud machine. Something running only on your laptop, such as a local preview server, will need to start again there.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-cli.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: Pending edits can travel with the handoff. Keep the practice change on its own branch and inspect the changed files first.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: Read Essential Commands to start the CLI. Hand off to cloud Devins lists what travels. Devin Auth explains the role needed for enterprise sign-in.

title: Devin Apps · Share an internal tool with the right people
summary: Build a tiny web tool and check who can open its link.

intro.what: A Devin App is a web tool that Devin builds and serves at a stable address. Visitors sign in to Devin.
intro.features: The Share control sets who can open it. Use a made-up dataset when testing a new app.
intro.exchange: Give the mail team a private page for a pretend queue count.
intro.m365: Let a small group try a list filter using sample rows.
intro.developer: Share a score counter with an invited tester.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: The Share control sets who can open it. Use a made-up dataset when testing a new app.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: In a practice session, ask for a Devin App with two sample rows and a count of the open rows.
Open the App. Compare the count with the rows. In Share, inspect General access before sending anyone a link.
For a limited trial, choose Only people with access. Check who already has access in that setting.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: A Devin App cannot be made public. It cannot register its own service worker, the browser helper a web app uses for offline mode.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-apps.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: A link alone cannot grant an outsider access. Count the people in the sharing list as well as the admins covered by the setting.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: Use Devin Apps for hosting, sharing and limits. Automations explains how a job can refresh a tool on a schedule.

title: Scheduled Devins · Run a check on a clock
summary: Set up a repeat report and see exactly when it will run next.

intro.what: A schedule starts work at a chosen time. New scheduled jobs use a Schedule trigger in Automations. Older schedules still run.
intro.features: Use a one-time practice run to check the job. Once the report is right, choose how often you want it to repeat.
intro.exchange: Count sample messages still waiting at the end of a shift.
intro.m365: Make a weekly list of practice tasks with no owner.
intro.developer: Check once a week that a game’s saved example still opens.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: Use a one-time practice run to check the job. Once the report is right, choose how often you want it to repeat.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: In Automations choose Create automation. Add a Schedule trigger and choose Run once for your first practice report.
Pick a future time and check the time zone. Give the job a tiny set of made-up rows and ask it just to report a count.
After the run, open its session and compare the count with the rows. Review the time zone again when setting up a weekly run.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: A clock can start a job. It cannot tell whether the report used fresh data or whether the answer was correct.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-scheduled.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: A weekly run at nine uses the chosen zone. Two people can read the same clock setting and expect different times.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: Read Automations for the current editor. Scheduled Sessions explains where an older schedule fits and how to move it.

title: Dynamic Workflows & Fleets · Test one project before many
summary: Give one practice project a change. Check its result before sending the rest.

intro.what: A fleet is a group of sessions doing related jobs. In a dynamic workflow, a script tells those sessions what to do and in what order.
intro.features: A workflow can send one job to each project. The script reads their results. A pass can unlock the next step. A failure can hold the other jobs for review.
intro.exchange: Try a mailbox column change on one sample export before rolling it out.
intro.m365: Move a sample team-list rule across two practice projects.
intro.developer: Test a save-file upgrade on one game before changing the rest.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: A workflow can send one job to each project. The script reads their results. A pass can unlock the next step. A failure can hold the other jobs for review.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: In an allowed session ask for a workflow that reads two pretend results. Give it a rule: if the pilot fails, stop before the next batch.
Try a failed pilot first. Ask which projects, if any, reached the next stage.
Change the pilot result to pass. The next projects should now be eligible for the next check.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: A fleet gives you more workers. It does not make a bad rule safe to repeat or decide what “pass” means for your project.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-workflows.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: A started session is not proof of a finished change. Record the project, branch and test result before moving to another batch.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: Read Dynamic Workflows for stages and saved results. Advanced Capabilities describes a parent session supervising other sessions.

title: Integrations & API v3 · Trace a request to one session
summary: Match the request in a chat or ticket to the work Devin starts.

intro.what: An integration lets another tool ask Devin to work. An API is a set of requests a program can send instead of someone clicking a button.
intro.features: In Slack, tag @Devin. In Teams, tag @Devin AI. In Jira, a ticket assignment, a mention or a label can start a job. An app can start one with POST /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions. Each connection needs to be set up first.
intro.exchange: Match a sample mail-report ticket to its session and test result.
intro.m365: Follow a request from a Teams thread to the session it opened.
intro.developer: Use a pretend game issue to trace one request and one reply.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: In Slack, tag @Devin. In Teams, tag @Devin AI. In Jira, a ticket assignment, a mention or a label can start a job. An app can start one with POST /v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions. Each connection needs to be set up first.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: Pick a practice Teams channel where Devin AI is installed. Mention @Devin AI and ask for a summary of one fictional task.
Look for the reply in the same thread. Match its session to the original request before sending another message.
For a program, read Create Session. The org_id in braces stands for your organization’s ID. The reply identifies the new session.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: A ticket alone cannot give Devin access to a repo. Creating a session does not mean that its work is finished.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-integrations.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: Save the session ID with the request. If a reply gets lost, look for that ID before starting another job.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: Read the guide for the channel you will use. Create Session gives the v3 request and required permission.

title: Enterprise Deployment & Outposts · Find where the work runs
summary: Separate the place that plans a job from the machine that opens its files.

intro.what: A deployment is where a service runs. With an Outpost, Devin plans in the cloud. A worker on your machine reads files and runs commands.
intro.features: With Enterprise Cloud, teams share the cloud, but each job gets its own machine. With a dedicated VPC, the host sets aside a private cloud network for one customer. With Outposts, your team runs the worker.
intro.exchange: Check which machine would read a pretend mail report.
intro.m365: Decide where a sample list export may be opened.
intro.developer: Choose a worker that already has your game’s test tools.

sections.title: What it is for
paragraphs: With Enterprise Cloud, teams share the cloud, but each job gets its own machine. With a dedicated VPC, the host sets aside a private cloud network for one customer. With Outposts, your team runs the worker.

sections.title: Do this first
paragraphs: Start with a diagram of the training setup: cloud planner, practice worker, sample folder. Draw a line from each job to the place it runs.
Read the Git rule in a sample security profile, the saved limits for a session. Work out whether that session can read code and push a branch.
Before a real run, ask your admin which worker and profile the session would use.

sections.title: What it cannot do
paragraphs: The plan still lives in the cloud. A worker can read a local file and still lack the right to push code.

sections.title: Plan and availability
paragraphs: {{fact.devin-reference-outposts.availability}}

sections.title: Gotchas
paragraphs: Ask two things. Who runs the machine? Where does Devin make the plan?
Git rules still apply on an Outpost. Your team must put the network rules into effect on its worker.

sections.title: Official docs
paragraphs: Read Enterprise Deployment for hosting choices, Outposts for worker placement, and Security Profiles for rules on what a session can do.
